utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the examination of witnesses, I'd like to make a few remarks. First of all, General Galic, you're here -- I'm glad you're here. I'm well informed some care has been taken of your problem yesterday evening.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't have the interpretation. But I understood what you were asking me, so I will answer. I hope I understood you properly. The prison doctor came to see me last night. He knows me well. He has treated me. And during this six months, he has managed to put me right. That is, I started walking within six months. So I trust him. But the most important thing is I don't want to waste too much of your time. But he said that because of the problems that I have, that I should be provided here a type of an armchair with an adjusted back so that I could rest my spine, because it is four or five hours that I have to sit here. Secondly, that in the cell -- I mean here in the Tribunal, as I wait, that I should be provided with a bed or again, a special armchair so that I could have a rest. Thirdly, that if I suddenly turn ill here, that there should be a nurse here who could give me an injection whenever necessary, that I should not be administered any stronger medicines than at present because it might affect my ability to follow the proceedings. Fifthly, he said that he would continue to consult with a neurosurgeon with regard to the operation and my general state of health because these three injuries -- these three spine injuries are quite questionable, quite difficult. And finally, we also talked about exercises which I should do. I do do exercises regularly, those which I can. And he said that he would convey it all to Mr. McFadden, so I'm seizing this opportunity to tell you all that happened, and that would be, in the nutshell, the conversation I had with the doctor during and after the examination last night. So thank you very much for your concern. I shall do my very best to be present at the proceedings invariably, in spite of the difficulty that I have or may have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we understand. We cannot solve your problems. The only thing we can do is to see that proper care is taken. If there's ever any need to inform us about health problems that are not properly taken care of, please inform the Chamber immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The second remark I'd like to make concerns the interpretation. Now and then we have some discussions about translations in either English or French, and perhaps sometimes differences of -- a few words that fall out. These discussions, we have them only because we have to do our utmost best to avoid any misunderstandings. At the same time, we have a great appreciation and admiration for the work the interpreters are doing. And during five hours a day translating simultaneously for people who very often have difficulties in slowing down is -- well, let me use the words, it's a hell of a job. And it's done by human beings. And of course we can't expect that it's always 100 per cent. If it's 99.5 per cent, that's already a great performance. And I'd just like to let you know that we are aware of it, and I hope you have understanding for the fact that whenever we see something which is -- well, within this last half per cent, that we have to take -- we have to pay attention to it. But it has got nothing to do with a lack of appreciation and a lack of admiration for the task you are performing. Then the third thing I'd like to do is to ask especially from Mr. Piletta-Zanin during the cross-examination of Mejra Jusovic who will enter the courtroom soon, to be very well aware of the fragility of this witness at this moment. As you see in the courtroom, there is a second chair next to the chair of the witness. That is because I allowed someone of the Victims and Witnesses Unit to sit next to her when necessary, even hold her hand, but of course not interfere in the cross-examination. You'll understand that it will not in any way affect the right of the Defence. But on the other hand, I have to take care that this witness will finally not come out with more perhaps psychological injuries where I think she had -- she has suffered already, a lot in the past. And I ask special attention to that from Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I think then, Mr. Usher -- Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. Good morning. Perhaps before the witness is brought in, I should like to make three technical comments which I think have to be dealt with before everything else. I begin about what you said last. It is evident, I believe, that you have all noted that the Defence when it interrogates, always does it with respect here. Mainly we always do it with the full respect for the witness. And we shall try to abide by the same principle and today even more than we did yesterday. My second point, Mr. President, has to do with a technical problem. I believe that we have received information about a map which was shown yesterday which we're asking about the origin of the map, what was the source, a technical one, because we only have the central part of the original document, and we're also asking the scale, the date, and all the other technical coordinates. I am raising this question because this matter was not resolved yesterday. And the third point that I wish to raise is the following: Yesterday in the afternoon or late afternoon, I believe, we received a ruling signed by Mr. Bruno Cathala, authorising the appointment on [indiscernible] Who was to make a statement with regard to the Article 92 bis. And we received this statement. I wish to say that the Defence has not yet spoken on the principle regarding the possibility of admitting specifically a report, or rather, this document which comes under Article 92 bis. And the Defence is somewhat at a loss because we see that the decisions are being taken, whereas we have not yet tackled the -- addressed the principle. So we do not know whether this will become the [indiscernible]. And before it is done, I'm afraid that we are putting the cart before the horse. It seems because this matter has not been resolved in principle. And fourthly, the fourth matter I wish to raise is the interpretation. Of course I do not want to question the quality of the interpreters and the work that they perform every day, which is very difficult work, and it is precisely because it is difficult that mistakes may -- may happen. And that is why we are formally asking, Mr. President, that -- it to be made possible to relisten the passages of the tapes, which I will point out to the registrar, if you allow us. And, specifically, if there are some passages, the passage concerning the witness that we heard yesterday and who I believe spoke about bullet casings, rather, and bullets in the garden or in the yard, that is what I believe I heard in this language. But I'm not entirely positive about this. And then the last witness that we had yesterday, it had to do with the fragment when she said that her husband was bearing arms. These are the things that are not entirely clear, and perhaps this point 90 -- point something per cent of the mistake that is we find in the rendition of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... May expect that the Prosecution will pay proper attention to that. As far as the third remark you made, we are bound by our own rules. That means that in the order of proceeding in 92 bis is that the statements first are obtained. That's what was referred to yesterday already by Mr. Ierace, which might be all not under all circumstance be the most satisfactory solution. But these are the rules at the moment. So this Chamber is seized by the 92 bis statements as soon as a request is there to have them admitted as evidence in this courtroom. And I can tell you that since we received the copy of the objections made until now by the Defence, that -- especially yesterday afternoon, I paid special attention how to proceed in this matter so that we can deal with it as soon as possible, as I indicated already in this courtroom. Then your fourth remark, I am not well aware of the -- of the procedure on how to consult the audio recording of the hearings. Madam Registrar, could you inform me exactly what the procedure is, if Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to hear in the original language one or two parts of the audio recordings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The request would go to the office of Legal Aid and Detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you know, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, where to address your request. And if there's any problem in having access to the audio record of the hearings, I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is a specific form you can request from Laurent in OLAD with the date of the recording you require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Living in a good bureaucracy, you see, there is a form that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, excuse me, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. President. So as to make everything quite clear, I will do that. I will ask it. But in the future, if our remarks are not quite right, if it turns out that our remarks were not completely wrong and that the witness pronounced the word "cartridge casing," and that the other one spoke about her husband Alta, will it be possible to correct the transcript, be it in French or in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'll seek proper information on how to do it. And as you know, usually I go to the registrar and see how it's technically done. But I'll take care that if it has been established that the translation was not complete or in every detail correct, and if you have drawn our attention to it, if it has been verified that one way or the other, but the transcript will be -- will be redacted. Having dealt with all the -- these problems, I think it's now time to ask the usher to bring Mejra Jusovic, accompanied by someone from the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Oh, let me just make one final remark: I noticed also that the 92 bis witness who has given a statement yesterday, I expect that -- is the statement available already, or -- and is the witness still in the seat of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the statement, in fact, has been available for some time. That is, the English version. The Defence has a copy of that. The difficulty with applying the proposed procedure to this witness is, as I explained two days ago, that we have the backlog of Sarajevoen witnesses who are able to return for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And so even if we were to obtain a ruling from the Trial Chamber in respect of Mr. Lindr and that ruling require him to give viva voce evidence, we could only do that in -- to the Sarajevoen witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have to deal with it in the near future and we cannot do it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I can tell you that the first witness beyond Mr. Kucanin is a witness who was to be dealt be by way of 92 is and with made him viva voce because of The opportunity available to us next week, that is Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mrs. Jugovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jugovic, The Chamber is fully aware of how difficult it is for you to testify in this courtroom. On the other hand, the Chamber hopes that you understand how important it is for us to hear from those who have been present. It's already a long time ago in Sarajavo on what happened exactly. We allowed you to be accompanied by someone of the Victims and Witnesses Unit, but it's not just her who's sitting next to you. Whenever there is any problem, please let me know immediately, and we'll take proper care. If you do not understand a question or if you say, "I need time to think," we're all there to assist you and believe me, your presence is of importance for us. I don't think it will take a long time. I think it will just take, perhaps, 10 or 15 minutes. So if you're ready to answer the questions, then Mr. Piletta-Zanin, who is Defence counsel, will put some additional questions to you. Yes? You are ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, thank you for giving me the floor once again. Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I want to personally wish you welcome in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very sorry that it happened the way it happened. I really was upset about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody can speak, and everybody here understood, and that includes General Galic. Everybody here understood what you felt and what you could feel. But there are certain questions which I have to ask you about matters which are quite neutral, so you can answer them without any fear whatsoever. And thank you very much in advance. Witness, I must go back to your statement. Is it correct that you made a written statement to or before the investigators of the OTP of this International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for this answer. Did you sign this declaration in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, will you please remind us, because your testimony spread over two days. But please remind us of the day when the incident happened. Did -- was that day a quiet day, or was it, on the other hand, very active, in military terms? We're talking about the 24th of July, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are. You mean when I was wounded by a sniper from Spicasta Stijena? Early in the morning around 6.00. I was wounded around 6.00. And I laid down for about half an hour there because nobody could come to me. But they did half an hour later and my neighbour called my son. And a friend of his who was killed later, and they took me to the hospital. They took out the bullet and took me back home, and then on a couple of -- and then a couple of times I had to go to have my wound attended to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, thank you for this answer. But my question was the following: That day when you were wounded, was it to your knowledge a day which was very quiet, or on the contrary, a day which was active in military terms? That is, whether there was any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shells fell that day, and there was a lot of fire, gunfire. And there were very many shells which fell that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, would you then agree with me that under the circumstances, the day when you suffered your incident was a day when the parties to the conflict were engaged on two opposite sides in military operations?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Witness. Witness, you said -- and I really tried to draw very precisely on my memory -- but you said that there were trenches in the area in the neighbourhood in which you lived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. I did not come out, because I spent time in cellars. It's -- I suppose it was further away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you see yourself with your own eyes these trenches, whatever their form? Were they just single trenches in -- sorry, trenches inside the soil, or were they elevated, made trenches?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was up there by the Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. But I asked you whether you yourself with your own eyes saw these trenches.

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for this answer. Did you see -- and we are talking about the entire war. So from May 1992 until September 1994, did you see there on that location soldiers or members of the army?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. When you say that there were soldiers, could you tell the Chamber if these soldiers were all in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not wearing uniforms. They did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us briefly how they were dressed, to the best of your recollection, of course.

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in different ways. They would have a blue suit, black, and so on, or white. They did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as far as you know, were there also women who were members of the army?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know more specifically whether in the logistics of the army -- and when I say "logistics," I mean procurement, food -- in this particular department, were there women involved?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, you said that you knew that there were soldiers in that area. Now, do you know where their barracks were, if there were any barracks?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the barracks were. It was just an empty area, open area. I don't know anything about that, because all this open area from the Spicasta Stijena was being targeted. We, the women from the cellar, we did not dare go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say that there were people who went in that open area or that empty area, according to the transcripts that I'm reading, what do you mean by "area," by that space, empty or open space?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an intersection that you could not pass at all because of the snipers. This was the most-targeted area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to your previous answer, you said that there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were people who passed through there. What do you mean when you say "people"? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people who lived in Sarajevo and people who lived in my street, in Sedrenik, probably these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say -- when you say "people," did you also mean soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, this area that you spoke about, this space that you mentioned a moment ago -- and I am just talking about page 12, line 14 -- did this area encompass the area where you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I understanding you correctly, if you say that there were no people who went through that area where you were wounded, but in a more general way?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just an open area, and it was very difficult to cross that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you be able to tell us absolutely whether soldiers went through that area or not?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. I will finish very quickly. I have another three or four questions. Witness, did you see in the area close to the confrontation line the demarcation line between the two parties, any kind of military station or a base where the soldiers could have gone to rest?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Now, could you tell us, where did these soldiers go to sleep?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if these soldiers slept in the trenches, or did they go to sleep in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, how long had you been living in this part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1964.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as far as you know, in the part where you lived, in the neighbourhood where you lived, were there men there who were soldiers at the time that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. A penultimate question, Witness: At the time of your incident, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you would like to know, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mrs. Jusovic, yesterday we saw that it was very difficult for you to answer all the questions, emotions coming up again. During the break yesterday and between yesterday when you finished your testimony provisionally until today, did you speak with Nazija Ocuz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've not been speaking with her yesterday when you left --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for you answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will now ask counsel for the Prosecution if they have any additional questions. Mr. Mundis, is there any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just another three or four questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis has another few questions for you Re-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Jusovic. On the morning you were shot, that is, July 24th, 1993, do you remember seeing any soldiers near the spot where you were at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any military equipment or heavy military weapons near the spot where you were at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jusovic, have you ever been in the army or worked for the army?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever worn a military uniform at any point in your life?

utterances.speaker: MEJRA JUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Jusovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I did not do it directly to the witness -- I did not ask the question directly because I did not want to upset her. But what happened yesterday is that we received some documents about the military activity in Sarajevo, about this particular date, 24th of July, 1993. And these documents, reports, by military observers. And I don't know whether I should show them to the witness. I don't think this is necessary, but I believe that it should be at the disposal of the parties and also your Chamber. And we would like to tender them as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Any objection even where this witness has not testified specifically on the documents themselves, but on the situation on that day to admit these documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like the opportunity to see the documents before I can comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, give copies of documents and perhaps since we'll have to decide, give copies to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Yes, everything is here. These are documents ERN number 0008421 and 8422, ending in such a way. They're two pages. These are observations on the -- for the 24th of July, 1993. On the UNMO in Sarajevo, these military observers of the United Nations in Sarajevo. And we have a number of shelling and firing and shots that take -- took place that day. And Mr. President, this is still the documents that we were given by the Prosecution some time ago. That is the source of the document -- or the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to these documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We'll decide on the admission in evidence of this document, which will, when we decide, will have what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D50. Would there be any additional questions from the Bench? No. We have no further questions to you, Mrs. Jusovic. That means that this is the end of your testimony in this Court. I once again would like to express the respect of this Chamber for your courage to come. We've all seen how difficult it was. It might even have been more difficult to re-enter this courtroom today, but I hope you are aware that everyone, all the parties and the Bench, is aware of how difficult it is to bring back into your mind those days that were very difficult for you and your family. Therefore, I'd like to thank you not only for coming from Sarajevo, but also for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... today, and I wish you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you so much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, would you please guide the witness out of the courtroom. And I thank the Victims and Witnesses Unit for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, thank you. I was rather troubled by this hearing, and I don't think that we -- it was noted in the transcript that when the witness indicated that she had the same type of hairstyle, is that we can perhaps say now -- give a description of her hairstyle to say that it was relatively short, that it did not come to cover her neck, and that it was above -- coming just below the ears. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a good description of the short haircut she had. I also had one remark, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. And please will you assist me. On page 13, line 15, could you please check the English transcript. As far as my recollection goes, you asked the witness whether she could, for sure, exclude the possibility that military people could pass through that area. But the translation says, "Witness will you be able to tell us absolutely where -- whether soldiers went through that or not." I think your question was whether she could exclude that they could have passed through that area. I'll check it in the French transcript, which I expect to include the word "exclure" which I noticed you used. I see you're nodding with me, and I assume that that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as a rule you know that the Defence can only agree with the Chamber, particularly when we're talking about these things. And yes, indeed, this was a double Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. negative, which was what I said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll keep that in mind when reading the transcript. Then we still have to decide on the documents tendered into evidence. Madam Registrar, could you please assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 360-degree Quicktime movie, P3279R, and the video P3280R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Defence Exhibit D50? Since there are no objections, they're all admitted into evidence. It's then, I think, up to the Prosecution to call its next witness, which, as far as I can see, would be Bogdan Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please could you bring in the witness, Mr. Usher. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I still wanted to thank you for the way you performed the cross-examination, the tone and the style in which you did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to make a habit of it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony in this courtroom, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Would you -- I invite you to make that statement. You have the text in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Vidovic, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Afterwards, you'll be cross-examined, if there's any need, by counsel for the Defence. And if there are any additional questions from the Bench, you'll hear from us. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please give the Trial Chamber your full name.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, in 1992, were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In November of 1992, did you join the police force in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, did you join the Centre for Security Bureau?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Criminal Department of the Security Services Centre, Criminal Service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you commence, say, a six-month training course which taught you about forensic techniques, ballistics, biology, chemistry, and the criminal law?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From February 1993 until July, that is, August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also do some study of photography, sketching, and fingerprints?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Everything that comes within the area of the criminal forensics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, did you essentially become a criminal forensic technician?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the basis of which I got a certificate, which says that I finished this course and yes, I am a criminal forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that training include working with senior officers so that you could learn from their experience?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of the lectures were done by experts, experts from biology, criminology, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your work involve investigating some shelling and sniping incidents in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Although -- yes. In any case, yes, that's what I did. It was just one of the areas of my work, apart from the ordinary on-site investigations when criminal offences were committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to sniping incidents, if there was more than one point of impact or entry point made by the bullet, did that give you any assistance in determining the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There are two methods by which you can determine this. For one more precise method, you need to have two points, that is, one entry and then one of impact. And then you can very precisely determine the place from which the shot was fired. And for the other method, you only just need one entry point, to then determine a direction from which the shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of June, 1994, were you required as part of your work duties to investigate a sniping incident involving a tram in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness be shown P2696, which is a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, would you please look at the document in front of you. Does it appear to be on the face of it a report made by an officer by the name of Numanovic in relation to the incident that you investigated together with some other people?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the investigations I did. And my colleague Numanovic at that time was a CID inspector, and this is his record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in that report, there are three named individuals involved in the investigation and you are one of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tavonje [phoen] is another fellow worker from the Criminal Investigation Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown exhibit P3655.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that General Galic cannot read his screen. I don't know if we have a technical problem or something. Just a moment. No, I think that the problem has to do with the video. We shall see now if it works. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there's nothing on the video -- at least not on the ELMO at this very moment. Is there? No. The ELMO is empty, so -- or is it the video channel that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to resolve the problem. Perhaps it is a misunderstanding. Mr. President, do we have on our screen something on the video -- I see. Well, then I'm sorry. So this was a premature reaction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Ierace, proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please go to the second page of the document in front of you now. Do you recognise your signature anywhere on that page?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes. This is my name here and the name of my colleague who did the investigation with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a signature alongside the name of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there are -- there is his signature and a signature of our boss, the one who checked, who controlled what we had done, I mean the report that we had prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can just clarify this for me: Is there actually your signature or just your typed name?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, only typed. This is done in two copies normally, so I guess I did not sign the second copy. I only signed one of the copies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, is this in effect your report in relation to your investigation of the tram shooting incident on the 16th of June, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of June. But yes, yes, that is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'll point out to the -- for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that again there appears to be a mistranslation. If one looks at paragraph 4 of the English translation, the second sentence commences with the words "on the 16th of June, 1994." If one looks at the Bosnian original, it seems that is the date in fact was the 19th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in that report, do you mention the names of the victims?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the names of the victims, the ones that we noted down when we went out to the site to investigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed is it apparent from your report -- and in combination with the earlier report, that your investigation was carried out on the day of the incident itself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown a series of photographs which are Exhibit P3656.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, perhaps you could reorder the photographs in front of you. Could you please go first to the photograph which has in the top right-hand corner numbers ending with "53."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's now on the ELMO. In your report, you say that the -- the particular tram involved had the garage number "236." On the photograph in front of you, do we see the number "236" Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stamped on the front of the tram? Perhaps you could point to it. Thank you. In other words --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it this was the tram involved in the incident. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please now go to photograph 51. And put that on the ELMO. Is that the same tram?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. It is the same tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Photograph 52; same tram?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Same tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on this photograph, do we see the same tram as indicated by the number "236" painted on the side of the tram? I think that appears alongside the windows.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the number here, the garage number of the tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before taking the photograph, did you place a sticker with an arrow and a measuring device alongside a hole in the side of the tram?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I put an arrow to indicate the point of entry in the tram that was hit, and the scale also just to show the scale, the size of the hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please point it out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please now put on photograph 49. Is that another photograph of the relevant hole?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was a close-up photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Photograph 50; does that show the exit point of the bullet on the inside of the side of the tram?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is. There is an arrow and a scale to show the size of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the red object which appears in the top left-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the back of the -- of a seat in the tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we look at that photograph, we see -- I'm sorry, I did say earlier the top left-hand corner. But I notice the way the photograph is placed on the ELMO, as we view the photograph on the ELMO, the red object is to the bottom right. And on the left side of the photograph, we see a greyish-coloured material. What was that greyish-coloured material? Which part of the tram?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is the central part of the tram more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't mean in terms of distance from the front of the tram. What I mean is: Is that the wall of the tram or the floor of the tram or something else?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what it should be. This is how it should be put. It is the part above the heater, and it is more or less level with passengers' feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please now go to photograph 55 and again on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, again to avoid whatever confusion. Since the ELMO was originally -- was on the screen with the number ending with "50," on the left-hand side, it has now been re-placed on the ELMO by the witness with the number just on top of the photograph and the arrow pointing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we now have on the screen the photograph ending with the numbers "55." If that could be placed on the screen. Could you position the photograph appropriately, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now it is placed correctly. This one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is indicated by the arrow which appears in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It indicates the place of impact of the bullet after it entered the tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did it hit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It hit the carrying frame of the seat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The carrying frame. Is that in effect the portion underneath the seat?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is underneath the seat. It supported the leg of the seat. Let me just mention that in this part of that tram, where this seat is, there are two seats facing two opposite seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does it therefore follow that the bullet penetrated the -- the left-hand side of the tram, as one faces the direction in which the tram was going? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It went through the plate wall and hit a seat which faces towards the rear of the tram. I can show it to you on the photograph 54, which seat it is. It is the seat where you see this man, and it is -- he faces the rear of the tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point that out again, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think on that photograph you point to the left half of the window which is to the right of centre of the photograph. Having penetrated the wall of the tram, did the bullet then strike a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not think that we have the same thing before us. I think that the witness had circled the right-hand side, that is, the right-hand side window. Could the witness repeat the movement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just clear it up. The point of entry is on the outside of the tram, on the outside wall. The seat which was hit next, which was hit as the bullet entered, is on the right-hand side of the tram, and it faces the rear of the tram, because as I have said, in that part of the tram, there are two seats facing one -- each other. Perhaps it would be simpler if I drew it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think that there could be hardly any misunderstanding, although I think I know what confused you a bit. Mr. Ierace explained that the witness was pointing to the left half of the window which is to the right of the centre of the photograph. So he was pointing at the window at the right, but on the left half of this window. Just in order to clarify the issue, the witness was pointing at a person sitting near a window which is not on the side of the tram of which the photograph was taken but at the other side, a person who is facing in the direction of number 236 and who is sitting left from two standing persons and a sitting -- what appears to be a woman with a scarf. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I'll just ask you some more questions about that. Firstly, I think I understood that you said the bullet hit the right side of the tram. If you could imagine standing in the tram and facing up the tram towards where the driver is, in other words, towards the direction the tram is travelling, did the bullet hit on the left or on the right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the left. On the left-hand side of the tram is the point of entry. And after it entered, it hit the seat which is across that hole. And the damage is on the left-hand side of the support as you look in the direction in which the tram is moving, or rather, in the direction of the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you imagine standing in the tram and looking in the direction of the driver, did the bullet hit the seat support -- I'll withdraw that. If you could imagine standing in the aisle of the tram facing the driver, so that you have some seats on your left and some seats on your right, the bullet came in through the left side of the tram. Did it then hit the supports of the seats on your left, or did it travel across the aisle and hit the support of the seats on your right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It hit the seat support to my right. It is this. This seat is to my right, as I stand facing in the direction in which the tram is moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So therefore, the bullet, having penetrated the wall of the tram, travelled across the aisle before it impacted with the seat support; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as we look at the photograph on the screen, which is 55, and we look at the seat support, can you also see what appears to be a grille on the left-hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation should be "the aisle." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please put on the ELMO the photo with number 55 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not use the word "the aisle." I wonder what my friend is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think you used the word a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not in the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in the last question. I don't know whether Mr. Piletta-Zanin was referring to -- I'd suggest, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if there's any need that the translation be corrected, that we assist the interpreters. Would you please not do it directly to the interpreters, but through me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. The word was not properly interpreted, but the word used in French was "el," and I think it is "elle" and I think that is just a minor detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. And it was just used to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assist the interpreters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, please look on the photograph on your machine to your right, and you see that the bullet impacted on what appears to be a middle column that slightly tapers towards the top.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the side of that column, we can see some grilles.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose these are the ventilation openings that are in the tram here. Or for the heating you have these openings here, too. Behind this tin plate -- behind this tin plate are the heaters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now place on the machine photograph 56?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation. Yes, the interpretation -- in French it shouldn't be grille, it should be grille.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in following it on the English transcript. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin, perhaps if you just write it down with the page and line number on a small note and we'll take proper care and give it to the Chamber so that we pay proper attention to it. I have another question. Mr. Ierace, there seems to be a -- as far as I understood, your question was about any grilles on this column. And it was not quite clear to me whether the witness was pointing at the grilles on the column or at the grilles at the side of the tram. Could you please try to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, as you look at the column, please with the pointer indicate what appear to be two sets of grilles: one lower and one higher. Firstly the lower set -- I'll withdraw that. We have to go back a photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have to go back to photograph 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's where the confusion started.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, would you please circle the grilles which we can see on the column.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there another grille higher up?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, as you understood it, what was the purpose of those grilles?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ventilation and heating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, against the -- I withdraw that. On the wall behind the column, there also appear to be some grilles. Perhaps you can circle those with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand those grilles to serve the same or a different purpose?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same purpose, I suppose. As far as I know, behind this grille here are the heaters, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now go to photograph 56. Now, first of all, on that photograph, as indicated by the arrow, do we see the same point of impact of the bullet as on the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the left of the photograph, we see a pipe that is anchored by some bolts into the floor of the tram. And to the left and behind it, we see a dark object. Could you firstly point to the pipe which is bolted to the floor?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the dark object to the left and behind the pipe.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they are.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This -- this tube here is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt again, but I need -- there was a very precise question. I do not know. Whenever we have a problem with French transcript, shall I record that and report it to, or shall I intervene? For instance, here in the French transcript we see "point d' entree," when it was said, actually, the "point d'impacte," and there was a major difference between the two. And it is simply that we do not do the same work twice, because I will have to re-read the whole transcript, comparing it with my notes. This is a rather delicate matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: I think if you're making a distinction between point impact and the other word you used, my main concern is whether there could be any misunderstanding. The essence of the question was whether this was the same point of entry or impact, but the same, as has been discussed before on the other photograph, I think. So there finally would hardly be any misunderstanding that suddenly the type of this point would be a different one from the earlier photograph or from the earlier question. So I'd like you to distinguish between those imperfections in the translation which could cause serious misunderstandings -- confusion, and those that are just of minor importance. If they're in minor importance, please write them down, give them to us, so that we can deal with it. If you are afraid that confusion could be the result of the imperfection of the translation, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. I am checking. I believe that the question -- I can check it, of course -- but I believe that the question was about the point of impact, point d'impacte. And there is a major difference between the point of entry and the point of impact, because these two -- because it is these two points which allow us to establish the line where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we could not hear the end of the lawyer's comment because it overlapped with the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, page 33, line 12, where it is -- [In English] as on the previous photograph. [Interpretation] And it is precisely about a very precise question, and it cannot be interpreted with the point of entry because it is exactly the opposite, and therefore with your -- with your leave, I took the liberty to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that part of the testimony of the witness is about two different points: The point of entry and the point of impact. So I do agree with you that this distinction should be properly made while translating. So therefore, I accept that your assistance at this very moment and whenever it could not create confusion or whenever it will not have a snag in this case, it would not be of great importance. I'd like you to just give a note to us, because the translation, of course, that's the bottom line, should be as correct as possible. So thank you for your -- for your assistance, especially in this matter where it has some relevance to correct it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We're at the time, Mr. President. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I even forgot to look at the clock. You know how dear the clock is to me. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, would you please look at photograph beginning with -- I'm sorry, the photograph which has numbers in the top right-hand corner ending with "56." I think it is on the ELMO at the moment. Before the break, I asked if you could identify the dark object which appears to the left of the photograph behind the pipe. What is that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This, that can be seen on the photograph. That's part of the door of the tram, what you call the "dark object."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that photograph we can also see the floor of the tram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. This brown surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the floor, in front of the number "1," there appears to be an orange irregular-shaped object. What is that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These are parts of the bullet that entered the tram. So that would be the jacket and part of the bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see in this photograph the floor of the tram. It appears to be a brownish colour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can also see part of the heater --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ierace. Can the witness point out the irregular-shaped object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, would you take a blue marker pen and circle the parts of the bullet jacket that you have identified.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we can see that the floor of the tram is brownish in colour. And to the top of the photograph, we can see part of what you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have identified as the heating or ventilation system. And that appears to be more of a reflective metallic surface; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're now pointing to the parts of the heater and also the floor.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would you please go back to the photograph ending with the numbers "55," and place that on the ELMO. Again, in this photograph, we can see the brownish floor material, in particular just above the number "1" that appears in the left-hand corner. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above it, we can see the --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above it, we can see the shiny reflective metal which contains some grilles. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. To the top of the metallic grille, we can see what appears to be a flat edge which is parallel to the floor. That also has a grille. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean this here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You're now pointing to the middle of the top of the photograph. Would you move your pointer to the left of the top of the photograph, the left-hand corner. Further to the left. Yes, thank you. Do you see a grille which appears to be on a surface which is parallel to the floor? And if so, please point to it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This bit here. And this is also the -- the same thing. It is the protector for the heater. It's also a grille, and it's also to the side -- it's on the side of the tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take your black -- I'm sorry. Please take the blue marker and circle the top grille on the surface, which is parallel to the floor level.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it would follow that the surface you have just circled comes out from the wall of the tram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it comes from the wall. In fact, it continues onto the wall of the tram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would appear to be at a height just below the seat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately it's at that height, right underneath the seat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, please go back to the photograph which ends with the numbers "50," and please place that on the ELMO. You told us earlier that the arrow indicates the point at which the bullet entered the cavity of the tram. We can see in the bottom left-hand corner part of the seat, painted red; is that correct? Coloured red.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's part of the seat. And here is the entry point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see immediately beneath the seat a shiny metallic surface protruding from the wall of the tram.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is this here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the top part of the heater?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is the top part of the heater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it therefore follow that the bullet entered the tram some distance above the floor level?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed at a point, a matter of a few centimetres beneath the seat?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. Yes, approximately several centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of your investigation -- I withdraw that. At the time you carried out the investigation, was the tram moved back to where you understood it had been approximately at the time that it was shot?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For security reasons, the tram was moved about three stops further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand that the tram had received the shot in front of a church?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to the statements of the people who were in the tram at the time, the tram was shot -- was in front of the church when it was shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your forensic investigation, were you able to establish the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The shot came when we look at the direction in which the tramway was moving, it came from the left side from the direction of Grbavica and Vrace, that are located on that left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of June, 1994, in whose control was Grbavica and Vrace?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this period, Grbavica and Vrace were under the control of the army of Bosnian-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away from the tram at the time it was shot was the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you precisely in terms of the distance, but approximately about two or three minutes' walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness? Please proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. I am just gathering up my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I do apologise to my learned colleague. I seek your leave to ask one or two further questions which I have overlooked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm sure that you will get some extra time to go through your notes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. No, no. It's just you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you to my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, would you place back on the ELMO the photograph that ends with the numbers "51." You told us earlier that the investigation was carried out on the same day of the incident, that is, the 19th of June, 1994. And I take it these photographs were taken by you on that same date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on that day same. The photographs were on that same day, and yes, I took them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this photograph, we can see a number of people standing around and walking and likewise in photograph 52. Could you please place 52 on the ELMO. During 1994 and indeed 1993, under what circumstances did the civilians of Sarajevo walk around in this area as freely as we see in the photographs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to walk like this and together like this, they could only do it at the time of a truce, a ceasefire which was then declared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a ceasefire active on the night of June 19th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was, because the tram was driving, and it could only operate -- be operated when there was a ceasefire, so that people could expect that they could walk freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Mr. Ierace has no more questions? Oh, good. Thank you. Now, before I begin this cross-examination, I would like to indicate the following: We established at the very beginning of the intervention of Mr. Ierace, there were certain kind of leading questions, and the Defence did not object because the Defence believed that the debate can continue and can advance so that we couldn't interrupt all the time, and so that at the end of the day, I could summarise it all. And the Defence is certain that it could obtain the same attitude of the Prosecution. And so I may have to ask some questions that may have a certain -- more of a leading nature than usual, and this is just to get a balance of [indiscernible] that could be useful to the cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to perhaps clarify this issue, in the common law tradition, as I understand it, leading questions are not permitted during examination-in-chief but they are while cross-examining the witness. So therefore, I would say, although we do not strictly follow the common law tradition, I think that leading questions are such that they'll not be opposed to by the Prosecution. That's of course a different issue, as far as referring to earlier parts of the testimony are concerned, which of course have to be very precise. But I tell you this now because it's -- I don't think it's a favour by the Prosecution if they refrain from objecting against leading questions. I think they would not be very successful in doing so during cross-examine. On the other hand, why do I explain this to you at this very moment is that this, of course, will have its consequences when the Defence will present its case, because then I think objections against leading questions by the Prosecution during cross-examination of the witnesses might not be that successful. So that just to explain what still is in the back of those who come from a common-law tradition and which is a bit in the mind of this Chamber as well, although not coming from a common-law tradition, having some idea of what's in the mind of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. common-law tradition people. Please proceed. If I do misinterpret the common-law tradition, Mr. Ierace, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was going to say, Mr. President. I have not objected to a question by my friend because of his leading, and I will not. There are other issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you for your words. And that's exactly what the Defence believes. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, witness, good morning. Thank you for being here today. And I believe you gave a statement, a written statement to the investigators of the ICTY. First of all, it was on the 15th of November, 1995. Do you remember? Do you remember giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I will refer to the written statement as I am talking about it. You mentioned in this written statement that you obtained certain qualifications and profession expertise as a policeman and a police technician; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, you mentioned certain ballistic expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, this was one of the subjects that I had on my course that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I can see that you have several qualifications, but I would like to limit myself to the ballistics. Now, regarding the problem of ballistics, is it true, Witness, that a system using a string was used to -- the angle of the firing and the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is done if there are two points: Entry of impact and point of entry -- point of impact and point of entry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Witness. I would like to specify for the interpreters. If you can speak into if microphone so that we don't have any problems. Now, you said that there were two points: One of entry and one of impact. Now, Witness, what are the criteria, technical criteria, that link to the ballistic deviation that you know to be, according to your expertise?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think I did not understand the question. What kind of deviation do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, you will agree with me to consider the following: That when we have a bullet which goes through a first obstacle and then there is a possibility of deviation -- deviation is trajectory, sometimes it's called the ricochet. First of all, when it hit the obstacle, it's -- the speed is changed and then a deviation is possible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Now, in relation to this deviation, what are scientific criteria that you used to establish to use your expertise? Otherwise, how do you calculate this deviation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that it is a very technical question. But I think we can try and understand. If we have a projectile that is deviating from the point of entry and the point of impact, you will agree with me that we can consider that its trajectory can be changed, can deviate?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So if the trajectory is changed, what is the scientific criteria that you've learned about that are used to take into account these changes in the trajectory? If you don't know, then you can just say so.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what criteria is calculated, but it does depend on the type of surface that the bullet goes through, depending on the softness or the hardness. The softer it is, there will be less of a change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yes, we agree on the principle with you, but because that you -- you had several of these cases, what is the norm, standard, criteria that you used in establishing this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please assist me. You said, question: "...agree on the principle, but because you had several of these cases, what is the norm, standard, you used in establishing this?" Until now, I've not seen any establishment in this case of the trajectory exactly followed or calculated by the witness. So I wonder what the relevance would be, since there's -- I do not see anything, any conclusion, drawn by this witness on the issues you're questioning him about. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I believe that the witness is here brought by the Prosecution to prove -- to show that the shot could have come from a territory that was held by the Serbian side. So it seems that the witness was a team member of a team, one of the three, who would go to the site to establish where the shot came from. Now, the witness just told us that, depending on the two points, the point of entry and the point of impact, we would be able to establish what is the source of the shot. Now, what I'm saying is that if this point can deviate, what is the criteria used in order to establish the source? So the witness can either say he knows it or that he doesn't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
