I do not agree with you, [Microphone not activated] to the extent that the witness has said that they would not be the -- on the basis that one could calculate the origin of the fire. Because I think so you need far more for that, for example, what kind of ammunition you are using, a lot of other elements necessary to -- the only thing I see that the witness did is that he said is that, it came from the direction of where Grbavica and Vrace is. And I did not see any other calculation as far as the -- as far as the trajectory of the bullet was concerned. So what is in the mind of the Prosecution by examining the witness, might not be the same as what the witness testified, which is rather limited. He said it came from the left-hand side of the tram, and that's where the Grbavica and Vrace area is, without giving any further details as to how the trajectory of the bullet was calculated. I did not see any calculation at all. So -- but please proceed. I'd just like to make this remark that until now, I've seen nothing like calculations you're referring to at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But I asked the witness a question, and I'll see if I can find where it is. The witness indicated that he used a system of strings in order to establish the origin of this shot, and I believe that the Defence has the right to establish -- and that is, whether a bullet can deviate from its trajectory. My second point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence is entitled to find out whether the bullet has deviated from its trajectory because the witness is here in his capacity of a quasi-expert and secondly, the point of impact is not along the direct trajectory, that is, the line of fire. If we try to establish on the basis of the point of impact in order to establish the origin of the shot, we would be committing an error in this case because it can deviate. And that is why I'm asking you this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as an expert, and technically and hypothetically, at a horizontal distance of 1 kilometre, can you tell this Chamber on the vertical elevation, what is the distance represented by an angle of 10 per cent?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer to this question could best be provided by an expert witness. What -- I do not perform any ballistic expertise -- any ballistic analysis on the site. In our practice, this is done by official expert witnesses. I can establish the general direction of the bullet. That is what I was trained for. When it comes to something more specific, as you're asking me to do, in our case, only official expert witnesses could answer such questions. And it is the common procedure to answer, this especially when we're dealing with motionless objectings, which is not the case here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you very well. I agree. Thank you very much, Witness. Let us go back to the statement. Will you tell us, of the three persons figuring in the list of persons who signed and established a document attesting to this incident on the 19th of June, 1994 -- I'm quoting from memory -- which one of these three persons was the ballistic expert in the technical sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The official expert witness did not come out to the site because the direct object was moved from the site. So there was no need for his presence there. It sufficed to establish the general direction from which the bullet had come from. So none of these three persons. There was my fellow worker, a criminal investigation operative technician, and the head of the team. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Thank you for this answer. If I understand you right, if I sum it up, you are saying that in relation to the document that we are talking about, that is, the police report, there is no ballistic -- ballistics expert. I'm referring to this document.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no expert witness there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness. Witness, to once again go back to this incident, you said that for safety reasons, your on-site observations were performed three stops further down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: About three stops further down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So about what distance from the site of the incident?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More or less. You don't have to be exact.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly three stops. How much it is in metres or kilometres, I can't really tell you exactly, and I'd rather not make guesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But you will agree with me, Witness, to say that we are a few -- several hundred metres away, rather than a few dozen metres away from the -- from the site?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know, Mr. President, is the microphone on all the time? I see that there is a delay, so I see that the booths have a problem. Is it all right with the booths?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the counsel and the witness could break between question and answer, then it would be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, may I ask you to -- not to answer very quickly. The interpreters have to translate whatever you say. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You were a policeman. And as a policeman, not only -- not a ballistics expert, and you were trained for that, but as a policeman -- and I should like to ask some questions that have to do with that profession at the time of the war in general, and we are referring to the period May 1992 to August 1994. The Bosnian army, did the members of the Bosnian army have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- I'm sorry. Can you please repeat the period of time you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The period of time that I'm interested in, Witness, is the one which covers the events, but primarily it is years 1992 to 1994: 1992, 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To begin with, I was not a member of the army. I was a member of the police. So I can the talk about the police. And what I can say is that at least one part of the police force had the police uniforms from before the war, that is, the same uniforms that the police used before that war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In your capacity as a policeman or a citizen in Sarajevo, did you -- could you see if soldiers wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were people who wore -- who did wear uniforms, uniforms which were, I should say, by and large made manually, made by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. I appreciate this last detail that you have furnished. When you say there were some persons, then ask a more direct question. Isn't it true that the vast majority of soldiers did not have military uniforms. And I'm quoting, which were not made by hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question. This question should be confined to a particular and far narrower point of time than the whole of the years 1992, 1993, and 1994. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please clear this up, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, Witness, I'm asking you the same question which you understood, but I am restricting myself to 1992. Then I will ask you the same question about 1993. And then the same question about 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The year 1992 includes the pre-war period and also the period where, according to other overwhelming evidence, there was not an organised army of the Bosnian government for at least some months after the conflict began. Thank you. The basic point is that the question is [indiscernible] in the present form and it should be restricted further, time-wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wise to do it more in detail at this very moment; otherwise we'll have to clarify it at a later stage. So could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after -- following the 4th or 5th of April, 1992, which I believe is when the war began, until the end of the year 1992, which I think is the 31st of December, 1992, was the army structure, did they have military uniforms which were not made by hand?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To begin with, let me repeat once again that I was not a member of the army. I was in the police. And the people who wore military uniforms were presumably on the front lines, and I did not go to them. I was in the city. And however, a vast majority of -- at least what I could see and what I heard, were uniform that is were made by hand, at least, that is what one could see following the media, following television. Whether somebody had a proper uniform or not, I really cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, but my question was to -- I wanted to find out whether there were official uniforms. And am I to understand, then, your answer as a yes, in the majority of cases?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Official uniforms? The police had them -- or rather, uniform that is the police inherited from -- from the former police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I spoke to you about military units. And you answered by talking about police forces. Is it that in your mind the military and the army units are one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police and the army. Well, listen, as far as I know, both the army and the police are the constituent around forces of the state. Having said that, one knows what the police does and that it is under the Ministry of the Interior. And the purpose of the army, as far as I know, is to defend the state borders and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for this answer. Can I then deduce from your answer that at the time when the police armed forces had official uniforms, that at the same time the military armed force did not have such uniforms? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992, I suppose people had uniforms that they could lay their hands on. And as for the police, the majority of the police, all the police had the blue uniforms that belonged to the police of the [Realtime transcript read in error"Serbian"] Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told me -- you are telling me that there were uniforms -- that people wore uniforms -- whichever uniforms they could lay their hands on. However, you are saying that in the vast majority of cases, there were no uniforms. And I think that you perfectly understood my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told that there is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, tell us what your problem is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said here and what I see here, I said that uniforms belonged to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I said Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you are following the English translation, Mr. Vidovic. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think now there are six of us checking whether there's any imperfection in the translation. You said the blue uniforms that belonged to the police of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what you said, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting us in avoiding whatever confusion. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, perhaps I could assist you, because I have the feeling that I know what you'd like to hear from the witness. And let me just see on whether we can get where I guess you'd like to be.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please wait for the previous speaker to finish before he takes the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talking about 1992 on from the moment where the conflict broke out and talking about those persons you considered to be members of the army of the Bosnian government. So at this moment I'm not talking about police forces, but -- of members of the army of the Bosnian government. What would they wear, let's say, in April, May, June, August, the rest of 1992? First the question: Would they wear uniforms, all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning, they did not. But as they went along, as they began to structure, then people tried to -- then make do. They endeavoured to look identically, that is, all the members of the army be dressed uniformly, even though I presume it was very difficult at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll go in much detail with you through these periods of time. So we're talking now about 1992, on from the beginning of the conflict. You said they would not wear uniforms. Was there a portion of those you considered to be members of the army, of the Bosnian government, have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, there was an effort to provide the uniformity, that is, to make uniforms for members of the army. Now, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Such an effort was made in 1992 to achieve an identical appearance of uniforms, because otherwise, people wore whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's my second question. When there were not yet uniforms provided to those people you considered to be members of the Bosnian government army, what would they wear if not uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Other civilian clothes which they tried to redo and make look like military clothing, to say, apply some camouflage patterns on them, or perhaps -- and sometimes used canvas. That was of that -- that was of camouflage patterns. Simply in order to achieve some uniformity of clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has there also been a time where members of this army would just be dressed in ordinary civilian clothing: T-shirts, jeans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But again, attempts would be made to have some kind of symbols on them. For instance, a piece of this patterned cloth as an armband or something, just to indicate that so and so was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate approximately the time in which you'd say that most of the members of the Bosnian government army would be clearly identifiable by their -- well, uniforms, although perhaps not official uniforms but their self-made uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. I forgot another thing when you asked me the previous question. There were also some symbols, or rather, an overwhelming majority of them had the symbol, or rather, the coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the then-coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When exactly they began to look uniformly, I wouldn't be able to say. But I think it was sometime in 1993. I wouldn't be able to remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that it took some time to get them uniformally dressed? You're indicating approximately one year. Am I correct in my understanding that ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well -- well, thereabouts, yes. Now, after all this time, I couldn't be more precise. I really couldn't. But let's say that that was -- that that was it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps one last question on this point, that is, the uniforms we're talking now, about 1994. Could you confirm of course if that was the case, that the official army, including the Territorial Defence, did not have uniforms for all of the -- for the whole force, for all the soldiers engaged?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in 1994, it was -- they all had a uniform look, that is, that they practically all had their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then be more precise. I'm talking about the official uniform, not something like it, but not about the appearance. I'm talking about the official uniform. Is that how you understand?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. If you call it that, the official uniform was the camouflage uniform, which army members wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate what were the colours of this camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was chiefly a combination of green and brown and beige. Perhaps something that would be just green with no pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. And I now go back. I will go back to the tram itself. The soldiers, did they have the right or the possibility to use these trams?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see why anyone should be exempt from using trams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, they had access to trams?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. At the time of the incident, that is, in June of 1994, on that date, did the Bosnian army have its own means of transportation? I mean, means of transportation of the troops. Did they have it in the town?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the means of all the transportation of their personnel? No, not around the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Witness, you lived in Sarajevo, and you discharged your police duties. Will you please tell us, which was the brigade which was territorially responsible for the area in which the incident happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the army brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only the military brigade, but also if need be, the brigade of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the incident happened in the Centar municipality. And in that part -- that part of the city, insofar as the police was concerned, it was the centre police -- Public Security Station, which brigade -- which brigade was responsible for that particular area, I really can't tell you with any certainty. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, in that case, tell us where was the nearest military command centre, the -- I mean, the nearest command centre of the army, the nearest one to the place where the incident happened. The military command centre.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know, once being a policeman, where this command centre was, the one that was nearest to the site of the incident? Is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you where the police station is and how far it is from the site of the incident; however, where the military headquarters were, I really can't be all that precise because perhaps I could indicate the part of the city, but where exactly they were headquartered, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us then start with that municipality and that police station; that is, these two different things. So consequently, Witness, where was the command post, the military command post centre? You said that you could indicate it but not very precisely, by perhaps indicating the part of the town where it is.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you precise the headquarters of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh well, now, if we take it in order, the 1st Motorized Brigade, do you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 2nd Motorized Brigade, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 5th Motorized Brigade, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The way the brigades were distributed, its distribution, they way they are positioned, I really couldn't give you a precise answer. I could tell you approximately where the lines were. But which brigade held which line, I don't think I could give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm not asking you who held which line but I'm talking about the headquarters. And you don't know anything about the 5th brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember which brigade that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, for the 1st Corps of the army, is your memory also not certain?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 1st Corps was located, as far as I can recall -- I think it was in the centre of the city, but I cannot quite recall the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the incident did take place in the centre of the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. At which distance was the police station from the place of the incident?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police station -- the police station centre -- police station centre cannot be seen from that place, because it's from the -- it's behind the buildings where -- from where the incident happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But at which distance? How far?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 200 to 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to confer a moment, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start with the line of -- I would like to go further. I'm going to go on to the line of questioning to do with the police structure a bit later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But now back to the investigation that you did, the on-site investigation with two other people who were not ballistics experts. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. now Witness, when this investigation took place, did you ask UNPROFOR forces or any other international forces to take part in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On some investigations, yes, we did have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about this particular incident in question. Did you -- yes or no -- propose to the UNPROFOR to be present there on site?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that I would receive the information to go to the on-site investigation, then those who would organise the team to conduct the investigation -- and I don't really know about this specific case, whether they asked UNPROFOR -- the UNPROFOR to also be present at the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, would you agree with me if you were not told -- you were not told that the UNPROFOR would be present at the site of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you informed at any moment that members of the UNPROFOR will take part in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because there were always in and about time, then it could be expected that they would be present at an investigation like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. Now, should I conclude that every time that there was a problem, you would be guided by a principle that UNPROFOR members would be present or assist at the investigation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, there were then UN monitors who were -- UN observers who -- who would come to the site of the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. Would you agree with me that the police authority did not consequently inform UNPROFOR authorities of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Perhaps the question could be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The word "consequently," is ambivalent. I'm not sure the question asks, and it could be misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think "consequently" could indicate a consequence in time, but also a consequence as far as logics are concerned. Would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will leave out the "consequently."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to what you told us, Witness, just a moment ago, is it true to say that -- that the authorities, the police authorities, as a general rule, did not inform UNPROFOR authorities of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Sorry, I think that we have a problem with the transcript. In line 62.14, I think that -- when it says "I think consequently," those are the words of Mr. Piletta-Zanin. [Interpretation] I believe that you said "donk", therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you -- these are your words. You have an excellent memory, so I'm inclined to trust it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it -- my second question, I did not use either "donk," therefore or "consequemment," consequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your first question, in the original question. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. May I ask another time in line 63 -- page 63, line 4 [In English] the words "you have an excellent memory," are your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think I should proceed, Your Honour. May I continue now with the same question? I'm not going to use anything like "therefore," or "consequently," or "thus."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, I asked you a question. Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that UNPROFOR was informed about every incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just said a moment ago, if I understood you correctly, that in this case -- about the case, the UNPROFOR was not informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know that that is the evidence. I don't recollect the witness saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please quote the source, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to this incident, the UNPROFOR, was it officially informed by the police authorities; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when such an information occurred, in which form would it be? Would it be written? Would it be verbal?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was done by the telephone. I'm sorry. I answered hastily. I think it was on the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, could you tell us, to the best of your recollection or knowledge, if the civilian or military authorities were informed of the incident -- Serbian civilian or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I did not understand the translation. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to repeat the question. Could you tell us if the civilian or military authorities, Serbian civilian or military authorities, were informed of the incident.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea. I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as a rule, generally speaking, is it normal that your police services where you worked, your police force, would inform civilian or military authorities -- Serbian military or civilian authorities of such an incident?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we were not in the courtroom. We were at war. So there was no such exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I did understand you. We're not in a courtroom, and there is no clash, conflict here. So I don't know why you're referring -- why you're making this reference. I'm just asking you to answer yes or no, if that is possible, to my question. Did you inform -- do you know about this? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. From our side, there were no -- there was no information given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much for your clear answer. That, I appreciate. Thank you. If we can continue in the same vein. Now, I would like to go back to the question of the tram. We could see that the tram was going in the Bosnian part of Sarajevo, Bosniak part of Sarajevo. Did this tram also go in the Serbian part or parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would be more appropriate for Mr. Piletta-Zanin to name those parts, rather than presume an understanding as to what parts were Bosniak and what parts of Serbian. That is an issue that's been in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To some extent it is. Not in all respects, as far as I can see. But if you -- if you would be able, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to be more precise on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to be even more precise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the war, the tram line that the tram that was involved in the incident followed, did it continue in the same direction I believe it was east-west or west-east. We would have to have a look at that. And how long did that tram line continue?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This tram went from Bas Carsija to Nedzarici before the war, which can be seen from its -- you can see that on it -- of its indication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we'll have a look at that, but before the war, the tram lines, did they go through certain areas which, at the time of the war, started to be considered as being Serbian areas? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those tram lines did not go through there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Thank you. I would like to go on regarding other elements of the police structure. And we would like to a little later show a map to the witness. Now, Witness, since you were a member of the police force, did you -- yes or no -- take part in combat operations, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, members of your police unit, did they -- yes or no -- take part in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, these members, did they take part in any way in terms of logistic support?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not. My department had nothing to do with combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the war, police units, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after the breakout of the war, what happened with weapons arsenals? What happened that belonged to the police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you as far as I know from the media, that some weapons depots were destroyed. But considering I was not a member of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police before the war, I don't know exactly which depots they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, my question was not related to before the war but after the war broke out -- or rather, do you know if police force were supposed to hand over their weapons to the military forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Do you know a unit that is known under the term of Vikiceva [phoen] unit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the name because he's known to the -- this is a commander of the then-special police force. But this is probably a -- a nickname or a slang word for the way they called that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, thank you for this answer, and I'm just saying for the transcript, this is Vikiceva unit. You said this was a special unit. Could you tell us what kind of a unit this was.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, this was a classic anti-sabotage unit, which had in its composition certain detachment for anti-sabotage, for prevention of -- of riots, and also for rescue -- and a detachment for rescue -- for mountain rescue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if I indicate that this special unit also had -- consisted of about 1.200 members, does this correspond to the facts?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this special unit have a -- a military unit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. This was just a special task unit, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does the name Zrak mean anything to you? Zrak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The name did not appear correctly, and I did not pronounce it properly. Is there a factory that was known as Zrak in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, Witness, do you know this factory?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know that such a factory exists in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree with me that this factory produced optical instruments?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was something like that. I -- yes, I think that that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I'm going to return to the special unit that we spoke about a moment ago. Is it true to say that these units could be armed with rifles that had sights, that were produced in the Zrak factory.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if within the police force there was a unit -- a Bosniak unit which was an anti-sniper unit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "no," does this mean that you don't know it or that it did not exist?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it, such a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, before looking at the map -- but I'm also looking at the clock at the same time -- I would like to ask you to give us some technical answers. Do you know how many men in 1993 and until the end of June 1994 were normally members of a police force -- the entire police force in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be able to give you an exact number. Perhaps approximate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you follow the training course which gave you extensive knowledge of police matters. Now, could you tell us how many police command posts there were in the city of Sarajevo, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was not an accelerated course. This was an ordinary course for criminal technicians. Now, as for the military -- as for the police stations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter correction --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Police stations, there were four. There was CSB, Security Services Centre, as the fifth. There was the building of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us with precision where these buildings were located that you just told us about.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could have a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. President, I have certain unmarked maps that are here. And for technical reasons, they will be produced in two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. May I remind you that the Prosecution took 52 minutes to examine the witness. You are now at approximately 73 minutes. Even if I were to deduct some time for technical problems -- although we had similar technical problems during the examination-in-chief as well -- could you please give us an indication as to how much time you'd still need, and could you also perhaps, but not too long, explain the relevance of all the police posts in town where this witness, I think, mainly was testifying about the incident with the tram. The first question was: How much time would you still need? I'm not going to say to you yes or no. How much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as little as possible. But at the moment, I would like to locate these points of -- on the map, as well as the front lines. If you ask me why I need that, then I will have -- take great pleasure in answering this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I say something at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- which could be relevant to this issue. The next witness is Mirsad Kucanin. He will be a long witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If we commence his evidence in the remaining 45 minutes, then it follows that is he goes over until Monday. On Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- the next proposed witness is Mr. Harding, who is in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If his evidence is delayed, it may or may not be convenient for him to wait in a wheelchair. We also have five or six other witnesses arriving on Monday night, which will clearly take us well into and beyond next week. The reason I raise these issues now is that I intend to make some inquiries and have some discussions over the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And it may be that I come back and respectfully submit that it would be inappropriate to commence the evidence of a fresh witness, that is, Mr. Kucanin, with only 45 minutes to go and with those inevitable consequences. The alternative, it seems to me, would be that we don't take -- we don't start Mr. Kucanin now so, that we can go on to Mr. Harding on Monday and perhaps put Mr. Kucanin over until a later time. But before I formally make that submission, I would be grateful to have the opportunity to meet with some members of my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. So as a matter of fact, you're saying that it might not be as inconvenient as it would have been otherwise if the cross-examination of this witness would take a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm quite surprised how the parties assist each other today, and I welcome it. So you don't have to answer my questions any more at this very moment. I urge that you do it as quickly as possible. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think it's wise to continue with the map after the break. If you would -- if that would be suitable to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am very glad to proceed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll break until five minutes to 1.00. I'll give you three minutes extra, because we are less in a hurry today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I just assume that you're going to inform the Court about what you found out. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do make the application that we don't call Mr. Kucanin today. I was able to speak to him during the break since there was not an interpreter available. But I did speak to some members of my team who informed me of some further complications. By not calling Mr. Kucanin today, we can then proceed with Mr. Harding first thing on Monday morning. And we may or may not call Mr. Kucanin straight after Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this doesn't change a lot in your preparations as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I have excellent news for the Prosecution. I shall be shorter than was envisioned. The problem was however the following: I'd like if possible that we do not change the order of witnesses for the simple reason that my colleague, who is also the lead counsel, is not here. We cannot therefore take a decision on this. And we have agreed to distribute the work, to share the work if possible. So obviously, if the order is changed, then I would like to be informed as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing, as far as I'm concerned, is that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would not start today with the next witness and then go on -- we'll see. Let's first finish the cross-examination of Mr. Vidovic and then see what -- what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will now show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these maps are exactly the same maps that we were using before. So this is a plan of Sarajevo. It's original in colour exists somewhere, but merely for simply -- for purely technical reasons, I will be using two photocopies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that you were going to say something, Mr. President. I saw that your microphone was on, and that is why I stopped. I made several photocopies, and I believe that only two, however, will be necessary. If, however, the witness wishes to mark something else on this other photocopy, in that case, I will produce three photocopies so that the maps will complement one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will now show you two photocopies that you will be able, with the help of our usher, analyse and then put them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say for the transcript, Mr. President, that these are the left and the right side of the same map that we produced for other witnesses. And I take the liberty of not attaching these documents so that we could have a frontal view of all of them, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you now to study these two documents. Witness, do you recognise a plan which is a reproduction of the plan showing the area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I suggest that we start with the map which mentions Novi Grad. And that is the left section of the map. Do you have it before you? Thank you. Very good. I see it placed on the ELMO. And let me just see if we have the same thing here. Right. Witness, on this map, can you show us where was it, to the best of your recollection, the place or the places which you mentioned before the break. You mentioned five or six locations of the police. Will you please point at these locations on the map.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Police stations, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meanwhile, usher, could you give the witness the marker -- the black marker, evidently. Could you please give it to the witness. I suggest, Witness, please, that you first -- wait, wait. Just a moment. Wait. Wait a moment. I suggest, Witness, that you first use the pointer. Will you then please point to them with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you repeat that gesture, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police Novi Grad police command, rather the Public Security Station, was here. In this area, here. This is part of the Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, will you please read out the name which you see here in this location that you have just indicated.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prvomajska Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is the street of the 1st of May. Will you now make a circle around that street using the black marker.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And put number "1."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Well, now do the same thing again, pointing on this part of the map, another station or stations, if there were any in this particular part of the city.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Novi Grad municipality, there was this particular police station. There were no other stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, and as for other municipalities, that is, on the same section of the map outside the municipality of Novi Grad, were there other -- or are there other police stations on the same map section outside the municipality Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I will then ask you a more specific question with regard to Alipasino Polje. Is there a police command post in that area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This part where I marked the police station, that is commonly known as Alipasino Polje. Or to be more precise, it is Srakino Selo, that is how it is known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So as to make things completely clear, will you then use the dotted line to indicate what you call Alipasino Polje. And if the usher would move the map up so that we can see better this part of this screen. Thank you. And it is now shadowed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it would roughly be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please circle it. Will you make a circle around this whole area of Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, at the bottom of what we see on the screen, would it be correct to say that it is the area or, rather, the areas, the localities of Dobrina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's where Dobrina is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. And in the area of Dobrina, isn't there a police command post?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a police department attached to the neighbourhood community -- I mean, in practically every neighbourhood community would be the patrol unit, a police patrol unit. I mean, these are patrols covering a particular neighbourhood community. So I wouldn't call it a command post. They have their --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, so we needed to look at something else. Will you please tell us how was the police structured, that is, is it true that there were police brigades; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was the police -- there were police who belonged to -- who were under police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it organised brigades like the military?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no brigades or battalions of the police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what police body did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the criminal investigations department of the security services, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was this centre organised, and to whom was it subordinated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was the head, the chief of the centre. And the centre basically covered the criminal investigation, that is, the criminal police department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the military police, was it something different from your police force?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please indicate on the map which are other command posts, including the Ministry of the Interior, which you mentioned before the break. And if the usher will help -- thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say, these are not command posts. These are police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the two maps don't coincide well, there is a centre part which is better reproduced, and I can also give it to the witness, if these two maps do not quite tally.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've found what I needed. Here was the building of the police administration of Novo Sarajevo, that is, that public security station. Then here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please circle the centre, and put number "2."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the street is ...?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says Enver Sehovic Street. But I don't know if it is the street. There's several small streets which -- the names of which are not indicated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now move on to points three, four, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the centre police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, number 3.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The street is indicated as number 22, so that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the name of the street? Is it the 22nd Street, or does it have a different name? What is the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about its name. And the "22" I suppose is some marking on the city map. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is true, Witness. But to the best of your recollection, what was the name of this street? Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, point four. Can you please point at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here is the Stari Grad police station. So that will be number 4. And the street is Logavina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to go back to number 3, couldn't it be Trscanska Street?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The street relative to number 3. Could it be the name of the street, Trscanska?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now move on to number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please make a pause after the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is where the centre -- security services centre is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you may not have heard it, but the interpreters have just requested that there be a pause between the witness's answer and the counsel's question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. I was listening to the French channel. May I ask both Mr. Piletta-Zanin and the witness to just wait until the proceeds, so that the interpreters can translate what you have been saying. So please slow down a bit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Ierace, for the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please continue. And I believe it has not been fully marked, the name of what you just indicated and marked as "5," what is this place and what is the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is where the security services centre was. The name of the street was Augusta Cesarca and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the current name of the street. Will you please repeat the name of the street for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Former is Augusta Cesarca Street? And now the street is called La Benevolencije. This is a very proper name for the secret service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can we -- will you now indicate other locations

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Republican Ministry of the Interior building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you also tell us which is the street. I don't think we've heard that yet.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what it was called before the war. Now I believe it is called Pruscak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, are there any other command posts, to your knowledge, linked to the police force?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These are all the police stations, the ones that I have just shown you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for clear answers. You told us previously that you could indicate the confrontation lines. I'm quoting you from memory. Could you do it now on a map. However, before we proceed, will you please take the pointer and indicate on the map, whichever map you prefer to use, be it the right section of the map or the left section of the map.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is now approximately, as far as I know. Not what I saw, but what I heard. It -- the line went more or less this way, somehow here, roughly now. I could, of course, make doodles around the map, but -- to circle it. It's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Witness. Since you've lived in Sarajevo, I think that your confirmation might be useful. Will you, then, do exactly that, that is, to erase but perhaps you should use a dotted line so that we can see which is the -- what was the location of the confrontation lines, to the best of your recollection, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness has just been asked to indicate on the map, to the best of his recollection, the location of the confrontation lines. That is, in spite of the witness in his previous answer saying his knowledge was based not on what he saw but what he heard, and that he could only do so approximately, therefore, I object to the witness being required to indicate on the map with a line the position of the confrontation line. It would be of no assistance to the Tribunal, given the state of this witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it might not have surprised you that I was conferring with my colleagues approximately on the same issue. Could you please clarify to us what the relevance is, apart from other problems, perhaps, with your question, as far as the map is concerned, what the relevance is of what this witness heard from other people on where the confrontation lines were. Is it because you want to know where the confrontation lines are, or is it because you want to check the reliability, whether the witness has heard it well from other people? Then I would expect that you will call the other people as witnesses. So in order to ask them what they said, where the confrontations lines were. Could you please indicate to us what -- what is the -- this exercise, what does it serve at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is because I think -- although I could perhaps find it in the transcript -- because the witness said at the very start of the cross-examination that he could perfectly well draw the front lines. And so I thought that because he had said it, that he knew partly because of professional reasons and because he's a policeman, that he probably found out because of his professional capacity, rather than personally, what is pertinent here. Also, we would like to remind that the incidents that happened on the confrontation lines, demarcation lines, and we note that sometimes they are confused with the trench lines. Since we've got enough time to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can please first indicate to me -- I'm trying to find it -- where the witness said that he was able to give the confrontation lines. And then perhaps if you say that the incident happened at the confrontation line, would we have to go through all the confrontation lines of Sarajevo, which I have to assume, after 32 days in court, that it might not all be on the map, which of course would create other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If you will authorise me, I will find the place where the witness said this. But perhaps we could ask him the question, whether this is according to his recollection. But I believe this is what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if he now says that what he knows about the confrontation lines is what he heard from other people, I mean, I do know that in this Tribunal, hearsay evidence is not as such inadmissible, but I still have some serious doubts as to what this will add to other evidence that this Court will hear and has heard already on where confrontation lines are. But just look first where he said it. I'm doing the same at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do it, Mr. President. But I would like to stress that in relation to the incident, the witness declared that the shot came from the Serb side. So he must have seen where the confrontation line was between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I've got no problem whatsoever if you ask the witness the confrontation lines near to where the incident happened. It's also clear what the witness said about what in his opinion was the source of the fire. So that would give us some guidance as to concentrate on what confrontation lines. But to go around the whole Sarajevo, I think is not that relevant. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you for a few moments so that I can find this place where the witness said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. What I found, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, now is on page 52, line 12, where the answer of the witness to your question was: "To begin with, let me repeat once again that I was not a member of the army. I was in the police. And the people who were -- who wear military uniforms were presumably on the front lines, and I did not go to them. I was in the city." I see no other "front," or "confrontation lines." I did use the search engine in this programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it can happen. This is one of the minor difficulties that we have occasionally, because we have three texts on the base of which we have to work. But maybe I could examine it later. I don't think it's that important. But I think that the witness said that he could, if he was asked to, to draw the lines of the front, the front lines. But perhaps we could see later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not my recollection, since the witness testified later on that what he knew about the front lines was about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. We can continue like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions that are related to the front lines near to the incident. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take the map that you have before you and locate the place of the incident and indicate for us -- if you can indicate the place of the incident.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The incident happened on the location of Marin Dvor, approximately here, up to the technical school. It would be approximately here, the area -- the location where the incident happened. The tram was coming from the direction of Bas Carsija. So it would be like this. Approximately here I could circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do not indicate anything on the map, please. Do not indicate anything on the map, please. Do not indicate anything. My microphone sometimes works and sometimes it doesn't, but I asked you not to indicate anything because I wanted to ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've just realised that on the copy of the map that I've been given, there are already some crosses and a circle. And they appear to be also on the map that the witness is marking. And I suspect that they're relevant to the same incident. I therefore say this, Mr. President, that especially given the questions the witness is now being asked, it is entirely inappropriate for the witness to be given such a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry. I apologise. I'm just looking at my maps. What are -- what are the circles that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, of course we see -- we see close to where the witness marked a "2" we see a circle around another line first. We also see just below the word "Marin Dvor," we see some old markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm so sorry, Mr. President. I'm very sorry. Again, I apologise. But this is the drama of the photocopier because we reused the same copies that we had prepared earlier. And I'm very sorry, because it is so faint that I couldn't see it. So I'm sorry. I thought this was a clean map. But in fact I do see a very faint circle going around [indiscernible], and I thought I was using a completely unmarked maps. I sincerely apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, are these markings such that you would oppose against the continued use of this map at this very moment, or -- I do agree with Mr. Piletta-Zanin, not that it is the drama of the photocopying machine but the drama of not taking out earlier markings. But as far as I can see, they are not of a nature which would very much influence the answers of the witness. But if you have of an opposite position ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't -- I don't have any further objection. In other words, I'm content for the Defence to continue to use the map in spite of my reservations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Again, I would like to reiterate my apologies to the Prosecution and to the Chamber. I think we used the old photocopies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on this photocopy, could you indicate in a line, a wavy line, could you tell us what you thought to be a line of separation, a demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately where, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? You'd say close to where the incident happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. That's what I said. "In relation to this incident." But I would -- did not want to lead the witness too much, in order to avoid any objection.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in this case, it was approximately near the Miljacka River, where the demarcation/confrontation line was. At the time, it was not possible to see it from this area. But I will approximately be able to draw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, Witness. If you can just mark the line.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the transcript, the witness is drawing a line, partially interrupted, partially broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps zoom in, please. The line is to the south of point number 3 and number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The very last thing: I would like to now have one of the photographs put on the ELMO, one of the photographs that the Prosecution showed you which shows the impact on one of the central pillars inside the tram. And I will indicate to you the number very shortly. The number given by the Prosecution on the exhibits, and this is 0217226 [as interpreted]. Witness, you said in your written statement that you were able to identify the projectile as having been able to come from where it came from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was from a side arm, a personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for this answer. Witness, this type of personal weapon that you told us about, can fire projectiles that we normally call "bullets"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The types of bullets that are used, are they -- do they end in a -- in a peak, or in a tip?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Do you mean this one in particular?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general. Do the -- are the bullets pointed, in general?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It depends which weapons we are talking about. For a rifle, they're mostly pointed. And for pistols, they're mostly rounded tipped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are we talking about a rifle that was used?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These are just parts of -- fractions of bullets, according to which it was impossible to say which kind of weapon was used. But this was then forwarded for further analysis. So I couldn't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, didn't you declare that from these fragments, bullet fragments, you were able to deduce that it was fired from a weapon of 7.9 millimetre caliber? Witness, didn't you say -- didn't you declare that this type of weapon could have been fired -- this bullet could have been fired from different weapons and from a M48 rifle, or a semi-automatic special gun that is designed as a sniper gun, or M-53, 7.9 millimetres caliber machine-gun? Didn't you say this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because it is a larger bullet, because of the fragments that were found, it is most probably this type of weapon, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Witness, so these were bullets that were pointed; right? And this was a rifle that was used; is that correct? Probably?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Now, this is my very last question. I would like to zoom to the point which is to the -- of the arrow, of the arrow. Not the circle. The point of the arrow, please, the tip of the arrow. To the tip of the arrow. This is still a circle and a number. Yes, here it is. This is the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please focus, put it in the centre, please. Go back a bit. Could you go closer, zoom. Zoom in. Could we have it clearer, please. Now, Mr. President, what I'm going to ask doesn't really come from the technical aspect. Yes, very much thank you. This is perfect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true to say that the impact that we can see 19 here --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] and Mr. President, this can be seen more clearly on the photograph --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is that this is not quite the rectangular form and is completely limited within this square? Could you look at the photograph 756, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd object to the question. It doesn't make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps my friend could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have another problem at this moment. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I know -- just wait. When we resumed, you said you had a good message for Mr. Ierace, and that would be that you'd take not much time. That was 50 minutes ago. You know the order of the examination of witnesses. That means that there should be a possibility to re-examine the witness, but the Prosecution and the Judges, if there are any additional questions, would be that we also have the opportunity. You also know that we are at the end of the week. We also know what problems we have, as far as the -- as far as the return of witnesses to Sarajevo is concerned. Nevertheless, you took 50 minutes, risking that the Prosecution would not be in a position to re-examine the witness, that there would be no time any more for the Judges. I do not understand this to be a good message. Well, the message was good, but the way you used your time was not good. Please put your question, make it short, avoid any unnecessary language in repeating and do it quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the trace square?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to the photograph, it looks as if it was a square, which is possible. It could have been. The bullet was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, is there any need to examine the witness? Yes, I now have to turn to the interpreters and to the registrar as well, whether we -- or if it would be possible to continue just perhaps for --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- three minutes for the Prosecution, perhaps a couple of minutes for the Bench as well. Would that be possible, or would this create insurmountable problems?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
