utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can continue in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Ierace, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Mr. President Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please place on the ELMO the map that you marked, that is, the one that shows Marin Dvor. You said earlier -- first of all, you were asked when you indicated on the map where the tram was. You had said earlier it was at the front of a church. Can you please locate the church on the map.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here. This is where the church is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please place an arrow with a blue pen pointing to that church.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were asked some questions about your opinion as to the size of the bullet and the types of weapons that it could be fired from. In your statement dated the 15th of November, 1995, did you say this: "We did locate small pieces of the bullet. According to the ballistics analysts, the bullet was a 7.9 millimetre. It could have been fired from several different weapons. They are the M-48 rifle, or a 7.9 semi-automatic special designed sniper gun, or M-53 7.9 millimetre caliber machine-gun"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing further. Oh, I'm sorry. Just one further question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions from the Bench? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you. While being cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you talked about using a string in order to establish what the direction of a bullet or projectile would be. Did you use a string in your investigation in this case, or were you referring to a technique used in these kind of investigations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a usual technique that is used. And here, this is -- was just used to put a link between the impact point and the entry point, because the tram moved from the place where the incident happened. Otherwise, it was used to determine the direction from which the bullet came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it had just been used to indicate where the point of impact and the point of entry was, without drawing any conclusions from that string exercise in relation to the source of the fire? Am I correct in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This can be calculated and is done by experts. And they also use another instrument. They use an optical instrument for that, in order to determine exactly the spot from where the shot came from. But of course if the -- the place from which it was fired is the place from which it was fired, we have two places, then it is possible to determine this. Now, if we have a bullet that comes into the room, then it is possible to determine. But in this case, you can determine the direction, but the tram moved from the spot from where it was hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you cannot make a proper calculation of where it came from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I could not point my finger exactly and say where the shot came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Vidovic, for answering all our questions. I would suggest to the parties that we first say goodbye to Mr. Vidovic and then deal with the other matters we still have to do. That means how we proceed next Monday, and of course the admission in evidence of the documents. Mr. Vidovic, you've come a far way from Sarajevo in order to answer all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You'll understand it's very important for this Court to hear direct from those who have been present during the events in the early 1990s and who were at the place of the events. So I thank you very much for having come to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- Mr. Usher, will you please lead the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The set of eight photographs, P3656; the report from the police station in B/C/S, P2696; and the English translation, P2696.1. The report from the public security station, in B/C/S, P3655; in the English translation, P3655.1. The two maps: The first map with one marking, I believe it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's D51. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the eastern part of the map of Sarajevo -- the Western. I'm mistaking. I'm sorry. It's the western part.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. And the second map, D52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With five numbered markings and one line on it. They're admitted in evidence. Then we still have to decide on how we proceed next week. Mr. Ierace, you told us that there were some problems in hearing the testimony of Mr. Kucanin. Could you please explain a bit more about it or when that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not yet been able to speak to Mr. Kucanin to discover his preferences. The situation is that the next witness, according to the order, is Mr. Kucanin, and then after him, Mr. Harding. We've made some inquiries of Mr. Harding in the last hour and a half, and he is able to stay until Wednesday. So that theoretically allows the possibility for Mr. Kucanin on Monday. However, Mr. Kucanin's estimate for evidence in chief is three hours, and it's likely to be that long. He has a lot to say. So Mr. President, at this stage, I would be grateful for the opportunity to make some further inquiries and then inform the Trial Chamber and the Defence within, say, the next two and a half hours of the order. It will be either Kucanin-Harding, or Harding-Kucanin, or Harding and then Kucanin goes over to a latter date. Whichever of those three options the Prosecution takes subject to the leave of the Trial Chamber should not impact too adversely on the Defence because they have been told firstly that the order is Kucanin-Harding, and secondly, that we proposed to call Harding at the beginning of next week. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. The Defence does not share the view of the Prosecution. My lead counsel in this case is supposed to prepare this weekend to hear the witness that was initially on the programme. And I'm not able to contact her this weekend. Also, I am not going to be able to do that either. So with no preparation is it possible for the witness that is being proposed instead of the initially proposed witness. So since we were not informed about this before, the Defence will not be able to accept this, and we would like to ask for the respect of the programme as it was established. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, who's going to prepare for the cross-examination of Mr. Harding? You or Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, to tell you the truth of the matter, we haven't yet had time to pay any attention to it because we knew that the witness would take a whole day or even more than a day. So we thought three hours for the Prosecution, then three hours for the Defence. So we haven't yet decided who would cross-examine the witness. So I cannot furnish you with an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just see what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is certain that none of us, neither my lead counsel nor myself, were ready for Mr. Harding. We haven't even read the documents. You would not -- we don't have any documents that would allow us to work on this; and I'm speaking for myself. So it is absolutely impossible for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'll give me just one second. You told us that your lead counsel in this case is supposed to prepare this weekend to hear the witness that was initially on the programme. That means that for the next witness, preparation still had to be made. I see that Mr. Harding has been announced to you as being heard on the 25th of February and at the 15th of February. I also do understand that you still have to prepare for your next witness. Let me just confirm with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I conferred with my colleagues, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. And we are now Thursday 2.00 -- until Monday morning 9.00 is three and a half days. You told us that neither the Defence have yet prepared the cross-examination of Mr. Harding but also not the cross-examination of Mr. Kucanin. I see that there are no exhibits indicated by the Prosecution for Mr. Harding. The Defence knows since the 15th of February that in the beginning of next week Mr. Harding would be examined. This Chamber allows the Prosecution to change the order and to start the examination-in-chief of Mr. Harding next Monday morning. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I did not say from what I see in the transcript -- I did not say that the Defence has not prepared its file for the cross-examination. What I said simply is that my colleague who is going to take charge of this has been working on it for some time and that she will continue to prepare herself over the weekend. What I have said is that I had no opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I did read your words literally as they appeared in the transcript. So there's no misunderstanding about what you said. I'm not saying that there has been no prior preparation from the part of the Defence, but the final preparation, which is still necessary to cross-examine the witness is -- it has to be finalised over the weekend. You told us that that had not been done yet, nor for Mr. Harding, nor for Mr. Kucanin. So therefore, we'll adjourn until next Monday. And Madam Registrar, usually on Monday we start not at 9.00, but at 9.30. So we'll adjourn until the -- until next Monday, 9.30. I think that's the 25th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
